Reading's population increased by around 18,500 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 170,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Reading increased by 11.9%, from just under 155,700 in 2011 to around 174,200 in 2021.

The population here increased by a greater percentage than the overall population of the South East (7.5%), and by a greater percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Reading was home to around 30.8 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 27.5 in 2011. This area was among the top 15% most densely populated English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was higher in Reading than across the South East

Median age increased

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Reading increased by two years, from 33 to 35 years of age.

This area had a lower average (median) age than the South East as a whole in 2021 (41 years) and a lower average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by around 6,200 (an increase of 28.7%), while the number of residents aged 4 years and under fell by around 1,700 (14.2% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 2.1 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Family in Reading

The percentage of households including a couple with dependent children increased in Reading, but fell across the South East.

In Reading, the percentage of households including a couple with dependent children rose from 19.3% in 2011 to 20.0% in 2021. During the same period, the regional percentage fell from 21.0% to 20.6%.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in Reading fell from 17.3% to 16.8%, while the percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children increased from 4.6% to 5.3%.

The percentage of households including a couple with dependent children in Reading increased by 0.7 percentage points

National identity in Reading

Reading saw the South East's largest percentage-point rise in the proportion of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK (from 17.8% in 2011 to 21.8% in 2021).

Cherwell saw the South East's next largest increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK (from 7.2% in 2011 to 11.0% in 2021).

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Reading increased by 4.0 percentage points

Rise in private renting

Reading saw the South East's second-largest percentage-point rise in the proportion of privately-rented homes (from 26.1% in 2011 to 31.9% in 2021).

Across the region, only Slough saw a greater rise in the percentage of privately-rented homes (from 24.3% to 30.7%).

Private renting in Reading increased by 5.9 percentage points

Reading residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 111,800 Reading residents said they were born in England. This represented 64.2% of the local population. The figure has decreased from just under 112,200 in 2011, which at the time represented 72.1% of Reading's population.

India was the next most represented, with just under 7,800 Reading residents reporting this country of birth (4.5%). This figure was up from just under 4,700 in 2011, which at the time represented 3.0% of the population of Reading.

The number of Reading residents born in Poland rose from just over 3,900 in 2011 (2.5% of the local population) to just over 4,900 in 2021 (2.8%).

In 2021, 64.2% of Reading residents reported their country of birth as England

Unpaid care in Reading

In 2021, 3.7% of Reading residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 6.5% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, 1.6% of residents (aged five years and over) reported providing between 20 and 49 hours of unpaid care each week, compared with 1.3% in 2011. The proportion of Reading residents (aged five years and over) that provided at least 50 hours of weekly unpaid care remained at 2.2%.

This area had the region’s second lowest proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care. Across the region, only Slough, with 3.3%, had a lower proportion.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Reading decreased by 2.8 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Reading

In 2021, 17.7% of Reading residents identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category, up from 13.6% in 2011. The 4.1 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the South East, the percentage of people from the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" ethnic group increased from 5.2% to 7.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 7.8% to 9.6%.

In 2021, 67.1% of people in Reading identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 74.8% in 2011), while 7.2% identified their ethnic group within the "Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African" category (compared with 6.7% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category increased from 4.0% in 2011 to 5.1% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.

Read the bulletin Ethnic group, England and Wales: Census 2021.

In 2021, 17.7% of usual residents in Reading identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category

Religion in Reading

In 2021, 36.3% of Reading residents reported having "No religion", up from 29.5% in 2011. The rise of 6.8 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Reading. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the South East, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 27.7% to 40.2%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 39.6% of people in Reading described themselves as Christian (down from 50.0%), while 8.9% described themselves as Muslim (up from 7.1% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

Read the bulletin Religion, England and Wales: Census 2021.

In 2021, 36.3% of usual residents in Reading reported having "No religion"

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of Reading residents aged 16 years and over, 45.5% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 43.1% in 2011.

In 2021, just over 4 in 10 people (40.8%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 41.8% in 2011. The percentage of adults in Reading that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership decreased from 7.5% to 7.4%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership was greater across the South East (2.9 percentage points, from 31.9% to 34.8%) than in Reading (2.4 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.3 percentage points, from 34.6% to 37.9%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Reading increased by 2.4 percentage points

Employment in Reading

Of Reading residents aged 16 years and over, 60.4% said they were employed (excluding full-time students) in 2021, a similar percentage as in 2011 (60.1%).

In 2021, just under 1 in 30 people (3.2%) said they were unemployed, compared with 4.3% in 2011. The percentage of retired Reading residents decreased from 14.4% to 13.6%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed fell from 59.0% to 57.6% across the South East. Across England, the percentage fell from 56.5% to 55.7%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Reading increased by 0.2 percentage points

Fewer adults working long hours

In 2021, 9.3% of Reading residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked over 49 hours per week. This figure decreased from 11.7% in 2011.

In 2021, just under 1 in 10 people (9.8%) said they worked 15 hours or less per week, compared with 9.6% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 62.9% to 65.2%.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked over 49 hours per week was greater across the South East (2.7 percentage points, from 14.6% to 11.9%) than in Reading (2.4 percentage points). Across England, the percentage fell by 2.2 percentage points, from 13.3% to 11.1%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults in employment who worked 49 hours or more in Reading decreased by 2.4 percentage points

Disability in Reading

In 2021, 6.2% of Reading residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 7.8% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under 1 in 10 people (9.7%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 9.6% in 2011. The proportion of Reading residents who were not disabled increased from 82.6% to 84.1%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot was greater in Reading (1.6 percentage points) than across the South East (1.0 percentage points, from 7.2% to 6.2%). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Reading decreased by 1.6 percentage points

Health in Reading

In 2021, 46.8% of Reading residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 44.3% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 36.7% to 35.6%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Reading residents describing their health as "very bad" was 1.0% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" fell from 4.0% to 3.7%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in Reading increased by 2.5 percentage points
